notes:
I've got verse notes for all of Amos 1, but they're uneven. Verses 1–5 are well covered; verses 9–10 and 14–15 rest mostly on one source. I hit my search limit before I could reach the Methodist, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox or bibleodyssey.org sites. So the tradition and "other views" sections are thin, and I left out anything I couldn't find on a page.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **Who Amos was.** His name means "burden" or "burden bearer," which suits a prophet whose message is mostly judgment. He seems to have had no formal prophetic training. He was a farmer called directly by God (Amos 7:14–15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **The word for "sheepherders."** The Hebrew word (*noqedim*) is rare. It appears again only for Mesha, king of Moab, a sheep breeder who supplied huge amounts of wool (2 Kings 3:4). https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary
- **Tekoa.** A small town in Judah about 10 miles south of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness. So Amos was a southerner sent to the northern kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary
- **"Which he saw."** Barnes says the Hebrew verb means a vision given by God. Amos calls them "his" words only to stress that he was the human instrument God spoke through. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-1.htm
- **The setting.** Both kingdoms were prosperous. Jeroboam II had pushed Israel's borders out further than at any time since Solomon. Underneath were luxury, oppression of the poor and empty worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary
- **The earthquake: how big.** Barnes says it must have been one of the greatest, since people still remembered it in Zechariah's time (Zech 14:5). He sees the two years as a warning and a time to repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-1.htm
- **The earthquake: no outside record.** Boice, quoted by Guzik, notes we have no record of it outside the Bible, so it can't help us date the book. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Amos lived to see it.** Coffman argues that dating the book by the earthquake shows Amos wasn't executed in Israel. He lived to see his prophecy confirmed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-1.html

**v. 2**
- **The lion's roar.** The roar is revelation, not just noise. The judgments that follow are God's own pronouncements, not the opinions of a shepherd. That is why Amos could face kings and priests without fear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary
- **"From Jerusalem."** Israel had set up rival worship centres at Dan, Bethel and Gilgal. Naming Jerusalem reminded them where true worship was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Pastures and Carmel.** As a shepherd, Amos knew how drought or invasion made pastures "mourn." Carmel may recall Elijah's victory over Baal there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Echoes of Joel.** Commentators link the verse to the same phrase in Joel and Hosea. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html

**v. 3**
- **"Three … even four."** This doesn't mean an exact count. It means sin piled on sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Barnes: the last straw.** The "four" is one more sin beyond a measure already full, the crowning sin that brings judgment. Only that sin is named in each oracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch.** The numbers simply show how many the sins were. They quote J. Marck: the guilt is full "to overflowing." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/amos-1.html
- **Gill.** "Damascus" stands for all of Syria. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html
- **Constable.** The word "transgressions" means rebellions against the Sovereign of all nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html
- **The crime.** Gilead belonged to Israel. Syria's treatment of it was like running a deep plough through the land. Hubbard, quoted by Guzik, reads the iron sledges as a picture of extreme cruelty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Was the threshing literal?** Chuck Smith says the Bible records Hazael actually doing these things. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html Precept Austin also discusses the possibility that threshing tools were literally used in war. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary

**v. 4**
- **Hazael.** Chuck Smith calls him the cruel king anointed through Elijah's ministry, and connects Ben-hadad with him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/c2000_Amo/Amo_001.cfm
- **Fire on the palaces.** Matthew Henry says royal palaces, however rich or well fortified, are no defence against God's judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary

**v. 5**
- **Breaking the bar.** Breaking the bar that held the city gate leaves Damascus open to the enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-5.htm
- **"Valley of Aven."** Barnes identifies it as the Bekaa valley between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/csb/amos/1-5.html
- **Aven as a pun.** "Aven" means "vanity" or idolatry. Some link it to the sun temple at Baalbek, much as Hosea mockingly renamed Bethel "Beth-aven." Keil says neither place can be identified with certainty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-5.htm Precept Austin suggests the name was a sarcastic jab, not a map label. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary
- **Calvin.** He sees a play on "trouble" (Aven) and "pleasure" (Eden). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-5.html
- **Henry.** Both the idolatrous and the pleasure-loving would be cut off together. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-5.html
- **Kir.** It was where the Syrians originally came from (Amos 9:7). The prophecy was fulfilled when Tiglath-pileser took Damascus in Ahaz's day (2 Kings 16:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-5.htm This happened in 732 BC. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-5.html

**vv. 6–8 (Gaza and the Philistines)**
- **What the crime was.** Boice, quoted by Guzik, says the sin wasn't war or slavery as such. Gaza enslaved whole populations (soldiers and civilians, young and old) and sold them to Edom for profit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Selling captives to an enemy.** Smith notes the captives were sold to Edom, Israel's long-standing enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html
- **The other cities.** Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron share Gaza's judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/

**vv. 9–10 (Tyre)**
- **Same crime, same punishment.** Tyre sinned the way the Philistines did, so it gets a similar judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Fire on the walls.** A city's walls were its strength, so burning them means defeat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- I found nothing on what the "covenant of brotherhood" was.

**vv. 11–12 (Edom)**
- **Edom as "brother."** Edom came from Esau, Jacob's brother, so the oracle can call it Israel's brother. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Nursing anger.** Guzik's application is to hand our anger to God and let Him avenge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **Poole.** Edom's anger was like embers raked into ashes, kept to be blown back into flame. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-11.htm
- **Gill.** The sins in view include Edom's idolatry, not only this one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-11.htm
- **Geneva Bible note.** Edom was a "continual enemy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-11.htm

**vv. 13–15 (Ammon)**
- **Geneva Bible note.** It stresses the cruelty of not sparing women, even though Ammon came from Lot, of Abraham's household. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-13.htm
- **Gill.** He counts their idolatry among the sins too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-13.htm
- **Guzik.** Ammon sinned against the future by killing babies in the womb. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/
- **v. 15.** The king and his princes go into exile together, because of Ammon's attacks on Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-1/

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

I didn't find any real denominational split on this chapter. The differences are between individual commentators:

- **v. 1, was Amos rich or poor?**
  - Calvin (Reformed) grants the word can mean a large flock-owner. But Tekoa was poor, he says, so a lowly shepherd was sent to shame proud Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-1.html
  - Matthew Henry mentions that some think Amos was a rich cattle dealer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-1.html
  - Gill (Baptist) thinks Amos was more likely a servant, which shows God's grace. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/amos/1-1.html
  - A modern devotional on Precept Austin calls him an educated rancher or agricultural businessman. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-1-commentary
- **v. 1, when was the earthquake?**
  - Calvin and Coffman pass on Josephus's view that it struck when Uzziah was struck with leprosy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-1.html
  - Gill argues the dates rule this out. Jeroboam would long be dead by then, so the earthquake must fall early in Uzziah's reign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-1.htm
- **v. 3, what do the numbers mean?**
  - Calvin: three plus four makes seven, a picture of Syria's growing hardness. He mentions and doesn't adopt another reading, "for three I spared; for four I will not." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html
  - Barnes: the fourth is the final, crowning sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/1-3.html
  - Henry: either "many" or seven, with the named sin always being persecution of God's people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Amo/Amo_001.cfm

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship (NET notes).** The earthquake was a well-known one in the first half of the 8th century BC. The notes argue the introduction proves Amos was a genuine prophet: he wasn't a prophet by trade or a northerner. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/download/netbible/ondemand/bybook/amo.pdf (I could only see an excerpt of this PDF.)
- **Catholic (translation only).** The Catholic Public Domain Version follows the Vulgate in v. 5: "camp of the idol," "house of pleasure," and Cyrene for Kir. https://biblehub.com/amos/1-5.htm The Pulpit Commentary also notes the Vulgate's "plain of the idol." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/1-5.htm I found no Catholic or Orthodox commentary.
- **Popular modern teaching.** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
